content.title: About
content.content: Whole wheat bread with raisins is a nutritious loaf made from whole grain wheat flour and sweet raisins. It has a dense crumb, a hint of natural sweetness, and a fragrant caramelized raisin aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole wheat bread retains all parts of the grain—bran, germ, and endosperm—making it more nutritious than white bread.
Raisins keep many of their antioxidants, such as polyphenols, even after baking.
Traditional Mediterranean recipes often include raisins in whole grain breads.
The high fiber content helps regulate blood sugar levels.
Raisins provide natural sweetness, allowing less added sugar in the dough.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Whole grain flour supplies a high amount of fiber, supporting healthy digestion.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: The bread provides thiamine, niacin, and folate, essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains iron and magnesium
items.content: These minerals aid muscle function and nervous system health.

items.title: Antioxidant properties of raisins
items.content: Raisins are rich in polyphenols that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: The combination of fiber and complex carbs helps you feel full longer.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Raisins increase the overall sugar level, which may be a concern for people with diabetes.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: The bread contains gluten and is unsuitable for those with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Wheat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to wheat.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Whole wheat raisin bread is relatively calorie‑dense; portion control is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the bread as a snack, for sandwiches, toast, or alongside soups and salads. Warm slices with butter and a drizzle of honey highlight the raisin sweetness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the loaf in a paper bag or bread box at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight bag for up to 2 months. Thaw at room temperature before use.

content.title: About
content.content: Focaccia is a traditional Italian flatbread made from a simple dough of wheat flour, water, yeast, salt and olive oil. The dough is allowed to rise, then baked until a golden crust forms. The plain version, without toppings, has a soft, slightly airy crumb and a fragrant olive‑oil aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Focaccia originates from the Liguria region, where it is known as “focaccia di Genova”.
Traditionally it is shaped into a flat slab and dimpled with fingertips before baking.
The classic recipe often includes olive oil, sea salt and rosemary, but the plain version keeps only oil and salt.
Focaccia is commonly served as an appetizer, used for sandwiches, or as a pizza base.
In Italy it has been called “the poor man’s bread” because its ingredients are inexpensive and readily available.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Wheat flour provides slowly released energy throughout the day.

items.title: Contains olive oil
items.content: Olive oil is rich in monounsaturated fats and antioxidants that support cardiovascular health.

items.title: Provides B‑vitamins
items.content: The dough supplies thiamine, niacin and folate, which are involved in energy metabolism.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: The light, porous crumb is easy on the stomach and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Low in added sugar
items.content: Unlike sweet pastries, plain focaccia contains virtually no added sugar.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Focaccia contains wheat, making it unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Because of the olive oil, the bread can be relatively calorie‑dense; portion control is advised.

items.title: Salt content
items.content: Traditional recipes use sea salt; individuals with hypertension should limit intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy focaccia fresh, cut into pieces and drizzle with extra‑virgin olive oil, balsamic vinegar, or pesto. It works well as a sandwich base, alongside soups and salads, and as a snack paired with wine.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store focaccia in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer storage keep it in the refrigerator (up to 5 days) or freeze it wrapped in plastic film and then foil.

green-beans-frozen-cooked-with-butter-or.title: Green beans frozen, cooked with butter or margarine

content.title: About
content.content: Green beans (snap beans) are young pods harvested before the seeds fully mature. Frozen beans are quickly blanched and flash‑frozen to lock in flavor, color, and nutrients. Cooking them in butter or margarine adds a rich aroma and improves absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Green beans are a good source of B‑vitamins, vitamin C, and potassium.
Blanching before freezing preserves the bright green color and crisp texture.
Thermal processing in fat increases the bioavailability of carotenoids.
In the United States, green beans are a classic side dish for Thanksgiving and fall meals.
Frozen green beans can be stored up to 12 months without significant quality loss.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports healthy digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood glucose levels.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C boosts the immune system and is essential for collagen synthesis, supporting skin and blood vessels.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium aids fluid balance and normal blood pressure.

items.title: Heart‑friendly profile
items.content: Low in saturated fat and rich in phytochemicals, green beans support cardiovascular health.

items.title: Improved absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins
items.content: Cooking in butter or margarine enhances the uptake of vitamins A and K present in the beans.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beans, ranging from mild skin symptoms to severe anaphylaxis.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Pre‑seasoned frozen mixes can contain added salt; people with hypertension should check the label.

items.title: Possible preservative residues
items.content: Certain brands use antioxidants to maintain quality; choose additive‑free options if you have sensitivities.

items.title: Overheating the fat
items.content: When sautéing, avoid overheating butter or margarine to prevent formation of trans fats and harmful compounds.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sauté the frozen beans in a skillet with a small amount of butter or margarine until tender, then season with salt, pepper, and your favorite herbs. Green beans pair well with garlic, lemon juice, toasted nuts, or grated cheese. They also make a quick addition to stir‑fries, soups, or pasta dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen green beans in their original packaging in a freezer at –18 °C (0 °F). After opening, transfer to an airtight bag and use within 3–4 months. Do not thaw and refreeze the product.

content.title: About
content.content: Jam (or jelly) is a sweet spread made by cooking fruit, berries or vegetables with sugar and sometimes pectin. It is commonly used as a topping for toast, pastries, desserts and sauces.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The term “jam” usually refers to a product that contains fruit pieces, while “jelly” denotes a smoother, gel‑like consistency.
Pectin, a natural thickener, is found in the skins and seeds of many fruits, especially apples and citrus.
In the United States jams are classified by sugar content: regular, low‑sugar and no‑sugar‑added.
Traditional English jam is often made from raspberries, strawberries or blackcurrants.
In some countries (e.g., Japan) jelly is made with agar‑agar instead of pectin.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Fruit jams retain some vitamin C, which supports immunity and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: A modest amount of fiber in jam with fruit pieces aids digestion.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Sugar provides a quick source of energy, making jam a convenient light snack.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Fruit components (berries, cherries, apricots) contain polyphenols that may reduce oxidative stress.

items.title: Enhances flavor of dishes
items.content: Jam and jelly add sweetness and aroma without needing large amounts of fresh fruit.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Most jam consists of sugar, which can contribute to weight gain and raise blood glucose levels.

items.title: Fruit allergy
items.content: People allergic to certain fruits (e.g., strawberries) may react even after cooking.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Some commercial varieties contain artificial preservatives and flavorings that may cause sensitivities.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The acidic nature of jam can irritate the stomach lining in individuals with gastritis or reflux.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Jam can be spread on bread, rolls, pancakes, used as a filling for cupcakes, pies and cheesecakes. Jelly is often served as a sauce for ice cream, cottage cheese or as a light dessert on its own.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store jam or jelly in a tightly sealed glass jar in the refrigerator after opening. When kept in a cool, dark place unopened, it can last up to 12 months. Discard if the product develops off‑odors, color changes or mold.

content.title: About
content.content: Noodle pudding is a dessert consisting of soft boiled noodles soaked in a sweet milk‑based custard. It is usually made with milk, sugar, eggs and flavorings such as vanilla or cinnamon. The pudding can be served warm or chilled.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The combination of noodles and sweet custard originated in Asian cuisines where noodles are often used in desserts.
Some regions add fruit pieces, nuts or caramel to the pudding for extra flavor.
Noodle pudding is often served in small individual cups, making it popular with children.
A rice‑noodle version exists, giving the dessert an even more delicate texture.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Eggs and milk provide a good amount of protein, essential for tissue repair.

items.title: Calcium
items.content: The milk‑based custard is rich in calcium, supporting bone and tooth health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Milk and eggs contain vitamins B2 and B12, which aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Quick energy
items.content: Sugar and carbohydrates in the pudding quickly replenish energy stores, useful after physical activity.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy should avoid the traditional version.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Large amounts of sugar can contribute to weight gain and increase the risk of tooth decay.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: If wheat noodles are used, the product contains gluten, which is important for those with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Noodle pudding can be enjoyed on its own, topped with berries, dried fruit or nuts. Serving it warm enhances its aroma, while chilled pudding offers a refreshing treat.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared pudding in the refrigerator in a sealed container for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze it in an airtight container and thaw in the fridge before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Shrimp scampi is a dish of large peeled shrimp sautéed in butter with garlic, lemon juice, and white wine, often finished with parsley. It features a bright aroma, a slightly tangy‑sweet flavor, and a tender seafood texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The word “scampi” comes from the Italian name for a type of sea‑crab, but in the U.S. the dish is traditionally made with shrimp.
The classic recipe uses only four ingredients: shrimp, butter, garlic, and wine.
It cooks quickly—usually 10‑15 minutes—making it a staple of fast‑service restaurants.
Scampi is commonly served over pasta, rice, or with crusty bread to soak up the sauce.
Variations add tomatoes, cream, or chili flakes for a different flavor profile.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Shrimp provide high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: A 100‑g serving of shrimp contains about 99 kcal, making it suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Contains omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: EPA and DHA in shrimp support heart and vascular health.

items.title: High in micronutrients
items.content: Shrimp are rich in selenium, zinc, and vitamin B12, important for immunity and nervous system function.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Astaxanthin, a natural antioxidant in shrimp, helps protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Shrimp are a common allergen; reactions can range from mild to life‑threatening.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Shrimp contain cholesterol, so individuals with high cholesterol should consume them in moderation.

items.title: Possible contaminants
items.content: In some regions shrimp may contain heavy metals or antibiotic residues; choose reputable sources.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Prepared scampi sauce often includes salt; people monitoring sodium intake should adjust accordingly.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot shrimp scampi over pasta, rice, couscous, or with fresh bread. Garnish with chopped parsley, lemon wedges, and grated Parmesan for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep raw peeled shrimp in the refrigerator for up to 2 days in an airtight container. Cooked scampi is best eaten within 24 hours; otherwise the sauce may separate. Freeze unused shrimp in a sealed bag for up to 3 months.
